b.include(send.build()); }, ) }

SqlxBroker::new takes the dialect built in for its pool's database; statements are built once when a subscription opens, the insert at compile time. A dialect builds the SQL of a broker's tables from their descriptions. The built-in one, BuiltIn<DB>, is the broker's default second type parameter: SqlxBroker<Sqlite> and SqlxBroker<Sqlite, BuiltIn<Sqlite>> name the same type. Each database has a feature that adds its dialect and its sqlx driver: postgres, mysql for MySQL and MariaDB, and sqlite. any serves an AnyPool by the built-in dialect of the database it reaches. A database without a built-in dialect is served by a dialect of the service's own. One struct describes a queue table on every database. The broker takes the dialect of its pool, which builds the claims and settlements of each subscription once, when it opens, so a message costs the same on every database. The derive renders the insert of every enabled dialect at compile time. The service writes its Publish per database, because that statement is its own SQL. What each database serves: Postgres MySQL, MariaDB SQLite AnyPool Row lock form yes yes no Postgres and MySQL backends Lease form yes yes yes no Advisory lock form yes yes in the process yes Isolation levels three four three modes the backend's listen_notify yes no no no Database clock statement_timestamp() UTC_TIMESTAMP(6) strftime(..), as text no time columns The connections a subscription holds depend on its form and on transactional mode, alike on every database: Connections shows how to size the pool.

The broker's type names the built-in SQLite dialect, the default of SqlxBroker::new. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_databases.rs use ruststream_sqlx::BuiltIn; /// One row of `thumbnail_jobs`, claimed under a lease. The same struct serves a `PgPool` and a /// `MySqlPool`: only its `Publish` is written per database. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "thumbnail_jobs")] struct MakeThumbnail { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<MakeThumbnail>::new("thumbnails"))] async fn thumbnail(image: &Image) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(path = %image.path, "making a thumbnail"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } // `SqlxBroker<Sqlite>` names the same type: the built-in dialect of the pool's database is the // default. fn broker(pool: SqlitePool) -> SqlxBroker<Sqlite, BuiltIn<Sqlite>> { SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<MakeThumbnail>("thumbnails") } fn service(broker: SqlxBroker<Sqlite>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("thumbnails", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(thumbnail); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_databases.rs use ruststream_sqlx::BuiltIn; /// One row of `thumbnail_jobs`, claimed under a lease. The same description serves a `PgPool` /// and a `MySqlPool`: only its `Publish` is written per database. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct MakeThumbnail { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for MakeThumbnail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("thumbnail_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for MakeThumbnail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Thumbnail; impl Handle<Image> for Thumbnail { fn handle( &self, image: &Image, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(path = %image.path, "making a thumbnail"); ready(Ok(())) } } // `SqlxBroker<Sqlite>` names the same type: the built-in dialect of the pool's database is the // default. fn broker(pool: SqlitePool) -> SqlxBroker<Sqlite, BuiltIn<Sqlite>> { SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<MakeThumbnail>("thumbnails") } fn service(broker: SqlxBroker<Sqlite>) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("thumbnails", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { let thumbnail = subscriber("thumbnails", Thumbnail) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<MakeThumbnail>::new("thumbnails")); b.include(thumbnail.build()); }) }

With the any feature, an AnyPool is served by the built-in dialect of the database it reaches at connect; its rows hold integers, text and bytes only. An AnyPool names its database by the scheme of its URL, so the service picks the database in its configuration and builds one binary for all of them. sqlx::any::install_default_drivers() registers the drivers before the pool connects. The broker picks the dialect when it connects, among the dialects whose features are on; another backend stops connect with SqlxBrokerError::Backend. A row holds the types sqlx::Any carries: integers, text and bytes, with no time and no JSON. A table on an AnyPool therefore has no locked_until, retry_after, processed_at or headers column, and the lease form is out of its reach. It serves the row lock form on its Postgres and MySQL backends and the advisory lock form on all three. A row lock table on a SQLite backend stops its subscription at startup, because the database is known only then. For the same reason a table's isolation level compiles at every level, and the backend's dialect refuses one its database does not open when the subscription starts, with SqlxBrokerError::Dialect. One Publish serves every backend when it writes the row through the derive's Insert on the connection the pool hands out. The AsyncAPI document describes the server by the URL's scheme, never its credentials. A test addresses the broker as tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Any>>().

An email queue in the advisory lock form, which every backend serves; the test runs it on SQLite in memory. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_databases_any.rs use ruststream::OutgoingMessage; use ruststream_sqlx::QueueDatabase; use sqlx::AnyPool; /// One row of `email_jobs` in the advisory lock form: integers, text and bytes, no time. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "email_jobs", advisory_lock = "email_jobs-{id}")] struct SendEmail { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i32, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// One insert for every database: the derive's own, on the connection the pool hands out. impl<DB> Publish<DB> for SendEmail where DB: QueueDatabase, Self: Insert<DB::Connection>, { async fn publish( conn: &mut DB::Connection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { let job = Self { id: 0, name: message.name().to_owned(), attempt: 1, payload: message.payload().to_vec(), }; job.insert(conn).await } } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("emails"))] async fn send(email: &Email) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, "sending"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: AnyPool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<SendEmail>("emails"), |b| { b.include(send); }, ) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // An `AnyPool` reaches its driver by the URL's scheme. install_default_drivers(); let pool = AnyPool::connect(&env::var("DATABASE_URL")?).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&pool).await?; service(pool.clone()).run().await?; pool.close().await; Ok(()) } examples/manual/sqlx_databases_any.rs use ruststream::OutgoingMessage; use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::{Column, KeyPart}; use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{Advisory, Attempt, Payload}; use ruststream_sqlx::{AttemptRow, InboxSpec, InboxTable, PayloadRow}; use sqlx::{Any, AnyConnection, AnyPool, Database, Postgres}; /// One row of `email_jobs` in the advisory lock form: integers, text and bytes, no time. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendEmail { id: i64, attempt: i32, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendEmail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Advisory, Attempt, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("email_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .group(Column::new("name")) .advisory(&[KeyPart::Literal("email_jobs-"), KeyPart::Column("id")]) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for SendEmail { type Attempt = i32; fn attempt(&self) -> &i32 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for SendEmail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// `sqlx::Any` hands a statement to its backend as written, so the insert names the /// placeholders of the database the connection reaches. impl Publish<Any> for SendEmail { async fn publish( conn: &mut AnyConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { let insert = if conn.backend_name() == Postgres::NAME { "INSERT INTO email_jobs (name, payload) VALUES ($1, $2)" } else { "INSERT INTO email_jobs (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?)" }; sqlx::query(insert) .bind(message.name()) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } struct Mailer; impl Handle<Email> for Mailer { fn handle( &self, email: &Email, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, "sending"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(pool: AnyPool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<SendEmail>("emails"), |b| { let send = subscriber("emails", Mailer).map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("emails")); b.include(send.build()); }, ) } #[tokio::main] async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { // An `AnyPool` reaches its driver by the URL's scheme. install_default_drivers(); let pool = AnyPool::connect(&env::var("DATABASE_URL")?).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&pool).await?; service(pool.clone()).run().await?; pool.close().await; Ok(()) }

SqlxBroker::with_dialect serves a database with a dialect of the service's own: Dialect, then the trait of each form it builds, and ByName for names. A dialect of the service's own serves a database without a built-in dialect, such as CockroachDB through sqlx's Postgres driver. Its type is the broker's second type parameter, SqlxBroker<Postgres, Cockroach>, and each thing its tables can do is a trait it implements: Dialect: names, placeholders, the statement that opens a transaction at a table's level, the savepoint a transactional handler's writes start after, and the statements every form runs to settle a row, move a dead letter, fetch rows and insert one; RowLock: the row lock form and its claim; Lease: the lease form, its claim, the extension of a lease in work and the stamp of a row a claim only selected; Advisory: the advisory lock form, its claim of candidates with their keys, the lock and the release of a key, and the take of a row whose key the session holds; Opens<Level>: an isolation level or SQLite mode a table may declare; ByName<DB>: subscriptions by name, the JSON headers and the times their rows hold. A table in a form whose trait the dialect lacks does not compile, and neither does a by-name mount on a dialect without ByName; the error names the trait. A dialect refuses with a StatementError what it does not build, such as FIFO groups, and the subscription of such a table stops at startup. The provided methods of Dialect and Lease state what their defaults mean for a database without the feature. The statements are built once, when a subscription opens, so a message costs the same as through a built-in dialect. A dialect may wrap a built-in one, such as dialect::Sqlite, and write one statement its own way. It then forwards every other method, the provided methods the built-in dialect overrides included, or the wrapped statements change. One statement written the service's own way is usually an event of the table instead, which needs no dialect. The crate registers the brokers of its built-in dialects with the test harness; a test of a broker on a dialect of the service's own registers its type once, with ruststream::register_testable_broker!(SqlxBroker<Sqlite, Audited>), and addresses it by that type, tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite, Audited>>().

The mysql feature serves MySQL 8.0.1 and MariaDB 10.6 or later in every form, READ COMMITTED by default; index the claim order so a claim reads its own group. Claims pass over locked rows with SKIP LOCKED, which MySQL 8.0.1 and MariaDB 10.6 added, and an advisory table shares that floor. A subscription reads the server's version when it opens, and an older server stops it with SqlxBrokerError::ServerTooOld. A claim's transaction runs at READ COMMITTED unless a row lock table declares another level. At READ COMMITTED a claim held for a handler locks no gaps between rows and holds back no insert into its table. A server whose binary log records statements (binlog_format = STATEMENT) refuses writes at that level; the row and mixed formats accept them. A lease claim selects its rows, stamps each one with its lease and commits. The expiry is a whole second, so a DATETIME column without fractions holds the token exactly. A dead letter into a table is two statements in one transaction. A claim of the service's own comes with a Fetch of its own, because the crate reads rows by a list of ids on Postgres alone; a subscription without one stops at startup. The advisory lock form takes GET_LOCK, whose names hold 64 characters at most. Index a table's claim order: (group, priority, retry_after, id), for the columns the table has. A row lock or lease claim locks every row of its group that it reads before sorting them. Without that index a claim held for a handler keeps the rest of its group from other claims, and in the row lock form the rows of a partition key go into work out of order. In a table with FIFO groups a claim first locks the unfinished rows of its group until its transaction ends, and the same index keeps that read to the group's own rows. A row lock table with FIFO groups that declares serializable stops its subscription when it opens, with SqlxBrokerError::Dialect: at that level InnoDB locks every row a read touches, and a claim would wait for the group's row in work.

Two groups share one table in the lease form, and the index (name, id) keeps each claim to its own group's rows. The tests run the same service on MySQL and on MariaDB. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_databases_mysql.rs /// One row of `welcome_jobs`, claimed under a lease. The claim stamps `locked_until` with a whole /// second, so a `DATETIME` column without fractions holds it. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "welcome_jobs")] struct SendEmail { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The claim order, `(group, id)` for this table's columns, keeps each claim to its group's rows. const SCHEMA: &str = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS welcome_jobs ( id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL, locked_until DATETIME, payload BLOB NOT NULL, INDEX claim_order (name, id) )"; #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("welcome"))] async fn welcome(email: &Email) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, "sending the welcome"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("receipts"))] async fn receipt(email: &Email) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, "sending the receipt"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: MySqlPool) -> RustStream { let broker = SqlxBroker::new(pool) .route::<SendEmail>("welcome") .route::<SendEmail>("receipts"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(welcome); b.include(receipt); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_databases_mysql.rs /// One row of `welcome_jobs`, claimed under a lease. The claim stamps `locked_until` with a whole /// second, so a `DATETIME` column without fractions holds it. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendEmail { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendEmail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("welcome_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .group(Column::new("name")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for SendEmail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The claim order, `(group, id)` for this table's columns, keeps each claim to its group's rows. const SCHEMA: &str = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS welcome_jobs ( id BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(64) NOT NULL, locked_until DATETIME, payload BLOB NOT NULL, INDEX claim_order (name, id) )"; struct Mail; impl Handle<Email> for Mail { fn handle( &self, email: &Email, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, group = ctx.name(), "sending"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(pool: MySqlPool) -> RustStream { let broker = SqlxBroker::new(pool) .route::<SendEmail>("welcome") .route::<SendEmail>("receipts"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")).with_broker(broker, |b| { for group in ["welcome", "receipts"] { let mail = subscriber(group, Mail).map_source(move |_| InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new(group)); b.include(mail.build()); } }) }

On Postgres every form runs: SKIP LOCKED claims, a one-statement lease claim, advisory locks on 64-bit hashes, statement_timestamp and LISTEN/NOTIFY. The postgres feature adds the dialect and sqlx's Postgres driver. The row lock and lease claims pass over rows other claims hold with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which Postgres 9.5 added. A lease claim is one statement: it locks the claimable rows, writes their lease and returns them. A claim of the service's own may leave the rows to the crate's fetch, which reads them by a list of ids. A table on the database's clock reads statement_timestamp(). The advisory lock form and the claims of FIFO groups lock 64-bit hashes made by hashtextextended, which Postgres 11 added. An older server refuses their statements, so their subscriptions stop when they open. An advisory lock belongs to the session that took it, so the advisory lock form needs a direct connection or PgBouncer in session pooling. A table that declares no level opens its transactions with a plain BEGIN, at the server's default. A row lock table works at read_committed; the stricter levels fail claims with serialization errors when claims and settlements of its rows run at once. Postgres runs READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, so its dialect does not open it, and a table that declares it does not compile. With listen_notify a subscription wakes on rows other processes write and announce. The AsyncAPI document names the server by the pool's host and port, never its credentials.

Invoices in the row lock form: each claim holds its row in a transaction while the handler runs, and four claims run at once. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_databases_postgres.rs /// One row of `invoice_jobs`. No lease and no advisory lock: the table takes its rows by row lock. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "invoice_jobs")] struct SendInvoice { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendInvoice>::new("invoices"))] async fn send(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(number = %invoice.number, "sending the invoice"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: PgPool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<SendInvoice>("invoices"), |b| { // Four claims in flight: each holds a connection of the pool while its handler runs. b.include(send.workers(nonzero!(4))); }, ) } examples/manual/sqlx_databases_postgres.rs /// One row of `invoice_jobs`. No `.lease(..)` and no `.advisory(..)`: the table takes its rows by /// row lock. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendInvoice { id: i64, attempt: i16, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendInvoice { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Attempt, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("invoice_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for SendInvoice { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for SendInvoice { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct SendInvoices; impl Handle<Invoice> for SendInvoices { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(number = %invoice.number, "sending the invoice"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(pool: PgPool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<SendInvoice>("invoices"), |b| { // Four claims in flight: each holds a connection of the pool while its handler runs. let send = subscriber("invoices", SendInvoices) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendInvoice>::new("invoices")); b.include(send.workers(nonzero!(4)).build()); }, ) }

The sqlite feature serves the lease and advisory lock forms in the service's process: one writer at a time, times as text, and no server to run in tests. SQLite locks the whole database for a writer, so no claim can hold rows for a handler. Its dialect implements no row lock form, and a subscription to a table without locked_until or advisory_lock does not compile. A lease claim is one UPDATE .. RETURNING that leases its rows, and one writer at a time keeps two claims apart. The rows of one lease claim come in no particular order. A claim of the service's own opens its transaction with BEGIN IMMEDIATE and comes with a Fetch of its own. The advisory lock form keeps its keys in the process, beside the pool. One process therefore serves a database file: two processes on one file may deliver a row twice. A table in that form needs no time column, so it needs neither chrono nor time. A transaction the crate opens takes the mode the table declares: deferred, immediate or exclusive. SQLite keeps times as text and compares them as text. chrono times sort exactly. time values sort right only across seconds, so with them a lease may end up to a second late, and a delayed retry may come back up to a second early or late (QueueTime). The AsyncAPI document describes the server by its protocol alone, with no host. An in-memory database named in a shared-cache URL, sqlite:file:<name>?mode=memory&cache=shared, serves every connection that names it and lives while one of them is open. A test runs the service on one with no server.

Thumbnails in the advisory lock form: two workers each hold a row's key in the process while their handler runs. A table takes rows by row lock unless it names another form: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a transaction held while the handler runs. A table takes its rows in one of three forms, and its description decides which: Form Selected by What holds a row in work After a crash Costs row lock nothing: the default the claim's transaction the row returns at once a connection per message in work lease #[field(locked_until)] an expiry written into the row the row returns when the lease runs out statements to claim, extend and settle advisory lock advisory_lock = ".." a lock on the row's key the row returns at once a connection per message in work A row lock claim locks each row with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a transaction that stays open while the handler runs. Rows that another claim holds are passed over, so claims of several workers and processes never wait for each other. The settlement's statement, a delete or the processed_at mark, commits that transaction, so a row and its outcome change together. The rows of a crashed process return at once, when the database rolls its transactions back. The price is a connection of the pool per message in work, held for the whole handler (Connections). Postgres takes the form from 9.5, MySQL from 8.0.1 and MariaDB from 10.6; SQLite has no row locks, so a subscription to a SQLite table that names no other form does not compile. On Postgres read_committed is the practical isolation level for the form: a claim at a stricter level fails with a serialization error when claims and settlements of its rows run at once. By hand, a description that calls neither .lease(..) nor .advisory(..) takes the row lock form.

Four workers issue invoices on Postgres; each holds its row's lock and a connection until its acknowledgement commits. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_forms_row_lock.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::PgPool; /// One row of `invoice_jobs`. No `locked_until` and no `advisory_lock`: the row lock form. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "invoice_jobs")] struct IssueInvoice { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The claim's transaction holds the row while the handler runs; the acknowledgement deletes /// the row and commits. A crash rolls the transaction back, and the row returns at once. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<IssueInvoice>::new("invoices"))] async fn issue(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.number, "issuing an invoice"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: PgPool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<IssueInvoice>("invoices"), |b| { // Each of the four workers holds a connection while its invoice is in work. b.include(issue.workers(nonzero!(4))); }, ) } examples/manual/sqlx_forms_row_lock.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::PgPool; /// One row of `invoice_jobs`. No `.lease(..)` and no `.advisory(..)`: the row lock form. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct IssueInvoice { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for IssueInvoice { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Payload,)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("invoice_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for IssueInvoice { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The claim's transaction holds the row while the handler runs; the acknowledgement deletes /// the row and commits. A crash rolls the transaction back, and the row returns at once. struct Issue; impl Handle<Invoice> for Issue { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.number, "issuing an invoice"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(pool: PgPool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("billing", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<IssueInvoice>("invoices"), |b| { // Each of the four workers holds a connection while its invoice is in work. let issue = subscriber("invoices", Issue) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<IssueInvoice>::new("invoices")) .workers(nonzero!(4)); b.include(issue.build()); }, ) }

advisory_lock = ".." holds each row by a lock on its key: rows that share a key go into work one at a time, and a crashed session frees its rows. advisory_lock = "video_jobs-{channel}" in #[inbox(..)] names each row's lock key: a placeholder names a field, the key reads its column, and the database renders the key as text. A key on the row's id holds each row alone; a key on another column keeps the rows that share it in work one at a time. A key belongs to the database, not to its table, so a key that starts with its table's name keeps two tables apart. A claim selects as many due rows as it may take, in claim order, each with its key. It locks each key on a connection of its own, without waiting, and passes over a key held elsewhere. Then it takes the row while the row is still claimable: the take counts the attempt and reads the row, and it commits, so a crash spends an attempt. The connection that holds the delivery keeps the lock, and no transaction stays open while the handler runs. A settlement runs its statement on that connection, where it commits on its own; then the lock is released and the connection goes back to the pool. retry() runs no statement: the claim counted the attempt, and the release returns the row. A delivery dropped unsettled releases its lock and closes its connection within five seconds, and its row returns. shutdown releases the lock of every delivery in work and waits for the settlements in flight (Shutdown). Each delivery in work holds a connection of its own until it settles, and a batch holds one row per key (Connections). Each database keeps the locks in its own way: Postgres locks a 64-bit hash of the key, and a lock lives in the session that took it, so the form needs a direct connection or PgBouncer in session pooling. MySQL and MariaDB lock a name with GET_LOCK: the database's name, a dot and the key, or its SHA-256 past 64 characters. SQLite has no locks a session holds, so the process keeps the keys in work, and one process serves a database file. A claim there reads the first due rows alone and takes nothing while they are in work, so a subscription has one delivery in work at a time, and with workers(n) each next row waits up to a poll interval. By hand, .advisory(..) takes the key as its parts, KeyPart::Literal text and KeyPart::Column columns, and Advisory goes into the description's type.

A video takes minutes to encode, and the videos of one channel go into work one at a time; an encode that fails returns its row with the release of its key. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_forms_advisory.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// One row of `video_jobs`, held by a lock on its channel's key while it is in work. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "video_jobs", advisory_lock = "video_jobs-{channel}")] struct Transcode { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, channel: String, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// A video takes minutes to encode. The delivery's connection keeps the channel's key while the /// handler runs, with no transaction open; a retry runs no statement and releases the key. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<Transcode>::new("videos"))] async fn transcode(video: &Video, Ctx(attempt): Ctx<keys::Attempt>) -> HandlerOutcome { if encode(video, attempt).await { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } HandlerOutcome::retry() } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("transcoder", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<Transcode>("videos"), |b| { b.include(transcode); }, ) } examples/manual/sqlx_forms_advisory.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// One row of `video_jobs`, held by a lock on its channel's key while it is in work. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct Transcode { id: i64, attempt: i16, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for Transcode { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Advisory, Attempt, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("video_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .advisory(&[KeyPart::Literal("video_jobs-"), KeyPart::Column("channel")]) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for Transcode { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for Transcode { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// A video takes minutes to encode. The delivery's connection keeps the channel's key while the /// handler runs, with no transaction open; a retry runs no statement and releases the key. struct TranscodeVideo; impl Handle<Video, (), (), InboxContext> for TranscodeVideo { async fn handle( &self, video: &Video, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, InboxContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ctx(attempt) = Ctx::<keys::Attempt>::from_context(ctx).await?; if encode(video, attempt).await { return Ok(()); } Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("transcoder", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<Transcode>("videos"), |b| { let transcode = subscriber("videos", TranscodeVideo) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<Transcode>::new("videos")); b.include(transcode.build()); }, ) }

#[field(locked_until)] selects the lease form: the claim writes an expiry and commits, the handler holds no connection, and the lease is extended. A claim writes the lease's expiry into locked_until, counts the attempt and commits at once, so no transaction stays open while the handler runs. The claim reads "now" once: the rows it finds due, the leases it finds ended and the expiry it writes start from that instant. The expiry is the delivery's ownership token: a settlement takes effect only while the row still holds it. While the handler runs, the subscription extends the lease of every delivery in work each half lease, and each extension moves the token forward, so a handler may run longer than its lease. A lease is how long a crashed process's row stays out of the queue: thirty seconds unless SqlxBroker::lease sets another for the broker or InboxQueue::lease for one subscription. It is whole seconds, at least one, and a shorter one is rounded up. A lease runs out under a running handler only when its extensions stop: the database out of reach, the subscription closed, the broker shut down. The next claim then takes the row, and the late holder's settlement fails with SqlxBrokerError::LeaseLost. A delivery dropped unsettled releases its row at once; a settlement whose statement fails keeps the row until its lease runs out, as a crash does. The claim counts the attempt, so a crash spends one too, and a delivery reports the attempt as it stood before its claim. After the broker shuts down, a delivery in work keeps its lease and settles as before, and the lease is no longer extended. The crate computes the expiry on the host, so the form reads the host's clock: locked_until beside clock = DatabaseClock does not compile. The column holds a time type, Option<DateTime<Utc>> here. By hand, .lease(..) names the column, and Lease<Time> in the description's type gives the lease's time type (LeaseRow).

A report takes minutes to render under a one-minute lease, which the subscription extends while the handler runs. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_forms_lease.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// One row of `report_jobs`: `locked_until` makes the table a lease table. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "report_jobs")] struct RenderReport { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// A report takes minutes to render. The subscription extends the minute's lease every thirty /// seconds while the handler runs; after a crash the row waits out its minute, then returns. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<RenderReport>::new("reports").lease(Duration::from_mins(1)))] async fn render(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { draw(report).await; tracing::info!(report.id, "report rendered"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<RenderReport>("reports"), |b| { b.include(render); }, ) } examples/manual/sqlx_forms_lease.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// One row of `report_jobs`: `.lease(..)` makes the table a lease table. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct RenderReport { id: i64, attempt: i16, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for RenderReport { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Attempt, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("report_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for RenderReport { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for RenderReport { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// A report takes minutes to render. The subscription extends the minute's lease every thirty /// seconds while the handler runs; after a crash the row waits out its minute, then returns. struct Render; impl Handle<Report> for Render { async fn handle( &self, report: &Report, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { draw(report).await; tracing::info!(report.id, "report rendered"); Ok(()) } } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("reports", "0.1.0")).with_broker( SqlxBroker::new(pool).route::<RenderReport>("reports"), |b| { let render = subscriber("reports", Render).map_source(|_| { InboxQueue::<RenderReport>::new("reports").lease(Duration::from_mins(1)) }); b.include(render.build()); }, ) }

custom(lock, unlock) hands the lock and the release of each key to the service's SQL, so a queue shares a lock another system already takes. The struct implements Lock and Unlock for its database. lock tries the key without waiting and answers whether it took it. unlock answers whether the session held the key; an answer of false, or an error, closes the connection, which ends the session and its locks. The two come together, and only in the advisory lock form; a description that breaks either rule does not compile. The dialect still selects the candidates and takes each row, so the claim keeps its order and counts the attempt as before. The process keeps no registry of keys for such a table, on SQLite too: the service's lock decides. A claim reads the first due rows alone and takes nothing while their keys are held, so the next row waits up to a poll interval. On Postgres a lock of the service's own is the place for pg_try_advisory_lock on a key another system computes; on SQLite it may be a table of the keys in work, as here. By hand, the chain adds .own::<own::Lock>() and .own::<own::Unlock>(), and the description's type lists own::Lock and own::Unlock beside Advisory. The other events of a table are on Events.

Billing holds an account's key in held_keys while it changes the account, and a payout of that account waits until billing releases the key. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_forms_lock.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::{Lock, Unlock}; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection, SqlitePool}; /// One row of `payouts`, held by the key of its account. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox( table = "payouts", advisory_lock = "accounts-{account_id}", custom(lock, unlock) )] struct Payout { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, account_id: i64, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// Billing holds an account's key in `held_keys` while it changes the account, so a payout /// never runs beside a billing run of its account. impl Lock<Sqlite> for Payout { async fn lock(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, key: &str) -> Result<bool, sqlx::Error> { let taken = sqlx::query("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO held_keys (key) VALUES (?)") .bind(key) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(taken.rows_affected() == 1) } } impl Unlock<Sqlite> for Payout { async fn unlock(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, key: &str) -> Result<bool, sqlx::Error> { let released = sqlx::query("DELETE FROM held_keys WHERE key = ?") .bind(key) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(released.rows_affected() == 1) } } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<Payout>::new("payouts"))] async fn pay(transfer: &Transfer) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(transfer.cents, "paying out"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payouts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqlxBroker::new(pool), |b| { b.include(pay); }) } examples/manual/sqlx_forms_lock.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use ruststream_sqlx::{Lock, Unlock}; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection, SqlitePool}; /// One row of `payouts`, held by the key of its account. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct Payout { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for Payout { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Advisory, Payload, own::Lock, own::Unlock)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("payouts", Column::new("id").generated()) .advisory(&[KeyPart::Literal("accounts-"), KeyPart::Column("account_id")]) .payload(Column::new("payload")) .own::<own::Lock>() .own::<own::Unlock>(); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for Payout { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// Billing holds an account's key in `held_keys` while it changes the account, so a payout /// never runs beside a billing run of its account. impl Lock<Sqlite> for Payout { async fn lock(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, key: &str) -> Result<bool, sqlx::Error> { let taken = sqlx::query("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO held_keys (key) VALUES (?)") .bind(key) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(taken.rows_affected() == 1) } } impl Unlock<Sqlite> for Payout { async fn unlock(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, key: &str) -> Result<bool, sqlx::Error> { let released = sqlx::query("DELETE FROM held_keys WHERE key = ?") .bind(key) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(released.rows_affected() == 1) } } struct Pay; impl Handle<Transfer> for Pay { fn handle( &self, transfer: &Transfer, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(transfer.cents, "paying out"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(pool: SqlitePool) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payouts", "0.1.0")).with_broker(SqlxBroker::new(pool), |b| { let pay = subscriber("payouts", Pay).map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<Payout>::new("payouts")); b.include(pay.build()); }) }

A headers column keeps a delivery's headers as a JSON object of strings; a publish with a header the column cannot hold is refused. #[field(headers)] marks the column, of type Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>> (feature json); by hand .headers(..) with HeaderRow, which lends the field. A claim moves the column's object into the delivery's header map, so middleware, ctx.headers() and the Headers<T> extractor read it as on any broker. In row mode the row a handler reads holds the column empty. The service's Publish writes the column, with HeaderColumn::from_headers over the message's headers. A JSON string holds UTF-8 text only, so a header value that is not UTF-8 would come back changed. Such a publish fails with SqlxBrokerError::Header before the service's Publish runs, and a header never reaches the table changed. A table without a headers column holds no header at all, and refuses a publish that carries one. A column of the service's own type implements HeaderColumn, and a table whose headers are columns of their own takes the headers layout.

The tenant of an export rides the headers column: the handler reads it with Headers<Tenant> and drops an export for a tenant the service does not serve. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_headers.rs use ruststream_sqlx::HeaderColumn; use sqlx::types::Json; #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "export_jobs")] struct ExportJob { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(headers)] meta: Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } impl Publish<Sqlite> for ExportJob { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { // The column keeps the message's headers as the delivery reads them back. let headers = Json::<BTreeMap<String, String>>::from_headers(message.headers()); sqlx::query("INSERT INTO export_jobs (meta, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(headers) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<ExportJob>::new("exports"))] async fn send_export(export: &Export, Headers(tenant): Headers<Tenant>) -> HandlerOutcome { if tenant.tenant != "acme" { tracing::warn!(tenant = %tenant.tenant, "a tenant this service does not serve"); return HandlerOutcome::drop(); } tracing::info!(export.report, tenant = %tenant.tenant, "exporting"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqlx_headers.rs use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{Headers as HeadersColumn, Lease, Payload, ProcessedAt}; use ruststream_sqlx::{HeaderColumn, HeaderRow, InboxSpec, InboxTable, PayloadRow}; use sqlx::types::Json; #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct ExportJob { id: i64, meta: Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for ExportJob { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<( ProcessedAt<DateTime<Utc>>, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, HeadersColumn, Payload, )>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("export_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .headers(Column::new("meta")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl HeaderRow for ExportJob { type Column = Option<Json<BTreeMap<String, String>>>; fn headers_mut(&mut self) -> &mut Self::Column { &mut self.meta } } impl PayloadRow for ExportJob { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } impl Publish<Sqlite> for ExportJob { async fn publish( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, message: &OutgoingMessage<'_>, ) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { // The column keeps the message's headers as the delivery reads them back. let headers = Json::<BTreeMap<String, String>>::from_headers(message.headers()); sqlx::query("INSERT INTO export_jobs (meta, payload) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(headers) .bind(message.payload()) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } struct Exporter; impl Handle<Export> for Exporter { fn handle( &self, export: &Export, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { let tenant = ctx.headers().get_str("x-tenant").unwrap_or_default(); if tenant != "acme" { tracing::warn!(tenant, "a tenant this service does not serve"); return ready(Err(HandlerOutcome::drop())); } tracing::info!(export.report, tenant, "exporting"); ready(Ok(())) } }

custom(fetch) reads the claimed rows with the service's own SELECT, such as a join; a claimed id it returns no row for settles by the decode policy. A message whose data lives in other tables lists fetch in #[inbox(custom(..))] and implements Fetch for its database; by hand the chain adds .own::<own::Fetch>(), with own::Fetch in its type. The fetch takes the claimed ids and returns the rows it found. Its SELECT returns the headers struct's columns under their names, locked_until included in the lease form, beside the message's own. The crate matches the rows to the claimed ids by the headers struct's id field, and an empty claim does not call the fetch. The fetch runs on the claim's connection: in the claim's transaction in the row lock form, and once per row, with that row's id alone, in the advisory lock form. A subscription to such a message does not check the message's own columns at startup, because the fetch reads them from wherever they live. A claimed id that the fetch returned no row for, such as a job whose order the join does not find, settles by the subscription's decode policy before the handler runs. The default policy drops the row, and the log names the id. A batch lends its handler the rows the fetch found, and the policy settles the others.

Each claimed job is read joined to its order; SQLite takes the claimed ids as a JSON array, read back by json_each. A job whose order is gone joins no row, and the default policy drops it. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_headers_fetch.rs use ruststream_sqlx::Fetch; use sqlx::types::Json; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// A job and the order it is for, read by the service's own fetch over a join. #[derive(Debug, Clone, Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(custom(fetch))] struct OrderMail { #[field(headers)] #[sqlx(flatten)] headers: MailHeaders, customer: String, total: i64, } impl Fetch<Sqlite> for OrderMail { async fn fetch(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, ids: &[i64]) -> Result<Vec<Self>, sqlx::Error> { // SQLite takes a list of ids as a JSON array, read back by `json_each`. sqlx::query_as( "SELECT j.job_id, j.locked_until, j.order_id, o.customer, o.total \ FROM mail_jobs j JOIN orders o ON o.id = j.order_id \ WHERE j.job_id IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(?))", ) .bind(Json(ids)) .fetch_all(conn) .await } } examples/manual/sqlx_headers_fetch.rs use ruststream_sqlx::spec::{self, Lease, own}; use ruststream_sqlx::{Fetch, InboxSpec, InboxTable}; use sqlx::types::Json; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::FromRow, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct OrderMail { #[sqlx(flatten)] headers: MailHeaders, customer: String, total: i64, } impl InboxTable for OrderMail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, spec::HeaderFields, own::Fetch)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("mail_jobs", Column::new("job_id").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .data(&[Column::new("order_id")]) .fetching(&[Column::new("customer"), Column::new("total")]) .header_fields() .own::<own::Fetch>(); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.headers.job_id } } impl Fetch<Sqlite> for OrderMail { async fn fetch(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, ids: &[i64]) -> Result<Vec<Self>, sqlx::Error> { // SQLite takes a list of ids as a JSON array, read back by `json_each`. sqlx::query_as( "SELECT j.job_id, j.locked_until, j.order_id, o.customer, o.total \ FROM mail_jobs j JOIN orders o ON o.id = j.order_id \ WHERE j.job_id IN (SELECT value FROM json_each(?))", ) .bind(Json(ids)) .fetch_all(conn) .await } }

HeaderColumn lets a headers column hold a type of the service's own; it moves the map in and out and names a header it cannot keep byte for byte. The trait has three methods. take_headers moves the headers the column holds into a header map, once per delivery as its row is claimed, so a column that owns its strings hands them over without a copy. from_headers builds the column value that holds a message's headers, for the service's Publish. unfit names the first header the column cannot hold byte for byte, and the broker refuses a publish that carries it with SqlxBrokerError::Header. The crate implements it for Json<BTreeMap<String, String>> under the json feature, and for Option<T> of any implementation, where None holds no headers. The trait is shared by the inbox and the outbox: one column type serves a queue table and an outbox table alike. The type is also a sqlx type of its own, so the driver reads and writes the column through it.

Lines keeps the headers one per line, name: value, in a TEXT column, and refuses a value that is not text on one line. ")) } fn unfit(headers: &HeaderMap) -> Option<&str> { // A value comes back as it went in when it is text on one line. let fits = |value: &[u8]| str::from_utf8(value).is_ok_and(|text| !text.contains('

Each field of a headers struct without a role is a header: strings and bytes as they are, numbers in decimal, times in RFC 3339, None left out. The header's name is the field's column name, as sqlx's rename and rename_all set it. Its value comes from HeaderField: Field type Header value String, Vec<u8> its bytes integers, bool its decimal text, true or false chrono::DateTime<Utc> (feature chrono), time::OffsetDateTime (feature time) its RFC 3339 text Option<T> the value of T; None leaves the header out A service implements HeaderField for a type of its own. A field of a type without it does not compile, and the error offers the impl or a role. The fields that play a role are not headers: the handler reads them on the message. The header map is built on the first read of the delivery's headers, by middleware or an extractor such as Headers<T>, and a delivery whose headers nobody reads never builds it. A message published into the table through a repository carries only the headers the headers struct names, and a publish with another header fails with SqlxBrokerError::Header, so no header is lost on the way into the table. By hand, HeaderFields builds the map with put_header, which writes each value through its HeaderField.

A shipment's headers are a carrier of the service's own type, an order number, a flag, a time and an optional trace; the handler writes them to an audit table as the header map holds them. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_headers_field.rs use ruststream_sqlx::HeaderField; #[derive(Debug, Clone, InboxHeaders, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "shipment_jobs")] struct ShipmentHeaders { #[field(id, generated)] job_id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, // Each field without a role is a header named after its column. carrier: Carrier, order_id: i64, express: bool, placed_at: DateTime<Utc>, trace: Option<String>, } /// A carrier, kept by its code in the table and named in capitals in the header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::Type)] #[sqlx(transparent)] struct Carrier(String); impl HeaderField for Carrier { fn header(&self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> { Some(self.0.to_uppercase().into_bytes()) } } examples/manual/sqlx_headers_field.rs use ruststream::HeaderMap; use ruststream_sqlx::{HeaderField, HeaderFields, put_header}; #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::FromRow, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] struct Shipment { job_id: i64, carrier: Carrier, order_id: i64, express: bool, #[schemars(with = "String")] placed_at: DateTime<Utc>, trace: Option<String>, } impl HeaderFields for Shipment { const NAMES: &'static [&'static str] = &["carrier", "order_id", "express", "placed_at", "trace"]; fn header_map(&self) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::with_capacity(Self::NAMES.len()); put_header(&mut headers, "carrier", &self.carrier); put_header(&mut headers, "order_id", &self.order_id); put_header(&mut headers, "express", &self.express); put_header(&mut headers, "placed_at", &self.placed_at); put_header(&mut headers, "trace", &self.trace); headers } } /// A carrier, kept by its code in the table and named in capitals in the header. #[derive(Debug, Clone, sqlx::Type, JsonSchema)] #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")] #[sqlx(transparent)] struct Carrier(String); impl HeaderField for Carrier { fn header(&self) -> Option<Vec<u8>> { Some(self.0.to_uppercase().into_bytes()) } }

In the headers layout a headers struct describes the queue table and its header fields, and the message struct that flattens it is what a handler takes. Two structs describe one queue. The headers struct derives InboxHeaders and describes the table: #[inbox(table, schema, advisory_lock, clock, isolation, mode)] and the fields that play a role, so it also selects the form. Its other fields are the delivery's header values. The message struct derives Inbox and holds the headers struct in a field marked #[field(headers)] and #[sqlx(flatten)], beside data of its own. It takes #[inbox(custom(..))] alone, and a role or a table attribute on it does not compile, with an error that names the headers struct as the place for it. The headers layout is row mode: a handler takes the message struct itself, or a slice of them in a batch. Several message structs may flatten one headers struct, each read by its own subscriptions. The claim selects the ids of the rows it takes, and the default fetch reads their rows from the queue table, the headers struct's columns and the message's own fields. A subscription prepares that fetch when it opens, so a message field whose column the table lacks stops startup with SqlxBrokerError::Schema. A message whose data lives in other tables reads it with a fetch of its own. The headers struct gets the generated insert, and the message struct gets none. By hand, one description on the message holds the whole table: .data(..) names the header columns, .fetching(..) the message's own, and .header_fields() builds the header map through HeaderFields and put_header.

A packing job: OrderHeaders describes order_jobs and its headers tenant, trace and order_id, and OrderJob adds the job's note. fn header_map(&self) -> HeaderMap { let mut headers = HeaderMap::with_capacity(Self::NAMES.len()); put_header(&mut headers, "tenant", &self.headers.tenant); put_header(&mut headers, "trace", &self.headers.trace);
